bible_refs.note: Sing to the Lord a new song, his praise from the end of the earth
If anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation. The old has passed away; behold, the new has come.
Reference to the song of Moses after the Red Sea crossing, echoed in the new song theme
Μακάριοι οἱ πραεῖς, ὅτι αὐτοὶ κληρονομήσουσι τὴν γῆν.
τὸ μάννα τὸ νοητόν, τὸν ἄρτον τὸν ἐξ οὐρανοῦ
τὸν ἄρτον τὸν ἐξ οὐρανοῦ, τὸν ζωὴν διδόντα τῷ κόσμῳ

choices.why: Perfect passive participle agreeing with understood subject; 'persuaded' fits the context of being drawn to worship, not merely 'convinced' which lacks the nuance of prior reluctance overcome.
Abstract noun from καινός; 'newness' captures the qualitative aspect of the renewal in Christ better than 'newness' as mere temporal newness, fitting the theological contrast with 'old things'.
περισπασμός literally means 'distraction' or 'over-occupation'; in context of life's turmoil, 'burdensome' conveys the weight and anxiety implied by the surrounding nouns 'wave' and 'disturbance'.

νοητός means 'perceptible to the mind' or 'intelligible'; here it modifies μάννα to contrast with physical manna, indicating the spiritual nourishment Christ provides, so 'intellectual' captures the noetic sense in theological context.
ἐπηγγελμένη is the perfect passive participle of ἐπαγγέλλομαι, 'to promise'; the land is described as 'promised to the saints', so 'promised' is the direct and accurate rendering.

pass_b_english: Those who were far from God have been persuaded to worship, and they will be called through the faith that is in Christ. They will come to know the King and Lord of all things, and the word shows this very clearly in prophecy.

For he commands those who have received mercy through God to glorify him, saying: Sing to the Lord a new song; let the beginning of it be praise, and glorify his name from the farthest corners of the earth—those who go down to the sea and sail upon it, the islands and all who dwell on them.

This song is new, and it befits the newness of the things that have come to be. For if anyone is in Christ, there is a new creation; as it is written, the old things have passed away, and behold, all things have become new.

Indeed, the children of Israel were ransomed from the greed of Egypt, with the wise Moses mediating at that time. They were freed from brick-making, from the empty sweat of earthly labors, from the harsh toil imposed by taskmasters, and from the inhumanity of their rulers.
They were led through the midst of the sea, ate manna in the wilderness, drank water from the rock, crossed the Jordan on dry ground, and were brought into the land of promise.
All these things are now new for us, and the old things are incomparably surpassed by what is better.
We have been set apart not for fleshly service, but for spiritual service; we have been separated from the earthly labors that arise from fleshly affection and from their pollutions.

We did not flee merely Egyptian overseers, nor even a tyrant who was impious and savage, except as a man among us. Rather, we have been turned away from those who urge us toward sin—wicked and unclean demons—and from the one who stands over their herds, that is, Satan.

We crossed through as if over a certain sea — the surge of this present life, its inner turmoil, and the truly burdensome distractions that pull us in every direction. We ate the intellectual manna, the bread that comes down from heaven, the very life given to the world. We drank water from the rock, having delighted in the spiritual gifts of Christ, which are clearly known to the intellect.

We crossed the Jordan, having been deemed worthy of the holy baptism, and entered into the land promised and fitting for the saints — a land which the Savior himself mentions, saying, 'Blessed are the meek, for they shall inherit the earth.' Therefore, in light of these new beginnings, it was necessary that a new hymn arise from its very source: from those who have come into being through him and who now begin their life in him. This hymn must be his fitting praise, not confined merely to the land of Judah, but proclaimed indeed from the farthest end of the earth to the other end, clearly encompassing all that is under heaven. For formerly, God was known only in Judah, and his name was great in Israel alone. But now, since we have been called through Christ to the full knowledge of truth, that knowledge has become complete.
